For some time now, my wife and I have contemplated sharing this story with that other site since literally everyone we know asks about this ordeal all of the time. But I was a little uncomfortable with the number of subscribers, and was unsure if I could handle it. Voat, however, appears to be less intimidating. I joined Voat in early June, but for the sake of protecting my privacy, I am using this username. Also, before I begin, I just want to be clear in saying that I don't feel comfortable sharing specific names of places or people (because I will be doing some shit-talking), but am more than happy to refer to them in general terms (i.e. "my wife," "hospital #1," etc.). As you can probably tell, this is lengthy, and I apologize in advance. I have never done an AMA before, so bear with me. Ready? Here we go:

In the late Spring of 2014, I had just graduated with a Master's degree, and my wife was working full-time while I was in the midst of job searching while supplementing our income by running an antique booth and piecing out my collection of vinyl records. I awoke one morning feeling absolutely awful. I was vomiting everywhere, I had become incoherent, I was dizzy, and sweating profusely. I knew that I needed to go the hospital, but I was unable to reach my wife as she was in a work meeting. It was hours before I got in touch with her, and when she finally arrived, I had passed-out naked on the floor. She rushed me to the hospital, but the events that would transpire over the next two months is entirely secondhand news. It was the last real memory that I would have until late August.

I would later find out that what had happened was that when passing a gall stone, it became lodged in my pancreatic duct, resulting in a life-threatening illness called "necrotizing pancreatitis." During this time, I would have "memories" -- we use quotes, because they weren't real memories, they were experiences based solely on perception. This is because my blood had become septic, and I began to have massive hallucinations. The illness itself was life-threatening enough -- I heard different reports from different people claiming that my chances of survival ranged from 15% to 50%, which means my survival was a coin toss, at best -- but the chances of dying were increased even more because the "reality" of my hallucinations were resulting in unintentional self-harm (including, but not limited to, ripping the central line to my heart, tearing the catheter into my penis with my bare teeth, and making escape attempts). For my own safety, I had to be restrained to a hospital bed. Because the condition was so serious, Hospital #1 had me transferred to a larger hospital an hour away (Hospital #2), where a specialized surgeon would be overtaking my case, placing me on life support and putting me into a medically induced coma. Despite my wife's full-time employment, we were uninsured, so she ended up having to deal with the potential that I would not live, while also navigating the bureaucratic healthcare system, because my hospital bills were getting higher and higher, and ultimately totaled approximately two million dollars. To make matters worse, both my wife and my father lost their jobs due to these circumstances, being so preoccupied with this. We were fortunate enough to be granted Medicaid, however.

Anyway, with so much damage being done by this illness, I had to undergo five major surgeries -- and I mean life-or-death surgeries, not the hundreds of procedures in between them -- and during my fifth surgery, I actually awoke in the middle of it because the anesthesia wore off. My internal organs were slowly dying, and they were forced to put me on dialysis and remove my gall bladder, my spleen, two-thirds of my pancreas, parts of my intestines, and parts of my colon. My abdomen would be split down the middle (think of two three-packs, instead of a six-pack) where I would have an open surgical wound in the middle, an ileostomy bag for pooping, a feeding tube into my chest, and a tracheostomy that prevented me from being able to speak. Also, being bed-ridden for so long caused atrophy in my legs, and I no longer had the ability to walk.

After spending five months between Hospital #1 and Hospital #2, I was then transferred to Hospital #3 for rehabilitation -- learning how to walk again, and doing basic things like putting on socks by myself. While Hospital #1 was average, and Hospital #2 was above average, Hospital #3 was an absolute hell-hole, in which I was coerced into consenting to unnecessary procedures, was kept uninformed about the status of my case, and even had nurses attempt to give me medications that I had not been prescribed, and was actually allergic to! I spent a few weeks there before finally being able to return "home". And by home, I don't mean the apartment that my wife and I had, but my parents' home, because my wife could no longer afford to pay rent after losing her job. Still, though, after spending 155 days in the hospital, I welcomed the freedom as if I had been incarcerated and was now on house arrest. I would still have a nurse visit our house twice a week to check up on the open surgical wound (among other things), and a physical therapist visited our home twice a week to help me learn how to walk again. A friend of the family also donated a Wii to us, so that I could play Wii Sports Resort, which had been recommended by my physical therapist.

The ordeal did not end there, however. In February, I had to go back to Hospital #2 for a sixth surgery, where they did an ileostomy take-down (no more pooping into a bag), placing a skin graft from my leg over my open surgical wound, and removing the feeding tube. Fortunately, this hospital stay was only eight days. But in late March, I ended up back in the hospital (Hospital #4) that is near my parents' home because I had been vomiting non-stop for a week. They found one liter of fluid that had collected in my abdomen, and they transferred me back to Hospital #2 so that my surgeon could oversee the case. In the meantime, my wife did find a better job, and we moved into a new apartment. Still, though, the ordeal did not end here. It took me over two months to find a general practitioner who would see me. I was turned away by all family practices in my city, and now have to drive out of town to see someone about my recovery. I might have even accepted this, except for the fact that we recently found out that my Medicaid has been deactivated, and we are now paying for doctor visits and medications out of pocket, in hopes that our re-application process will be approved. And this is a big deal because not only am I supposed to have a seventh surgery next year to have my abdomen reattached, but am in desperate need of seeing a psychologist to address the literal nightmares that I have every night and the figurative nightmares of dealing with all of this.

And this was all due to a single gall stone.

One more thing: my wife has been an absolute hero, and I think I would have died if she had not been there to take care of everything, and make the hard decisions and sacrifices that needed to be made, while carrying all of the weight on her shoulders. She is the love of my life, and I am so grateful to have her.

If you made it this far, thank you for reading. It was a lot longer than I had anticipated. But it's hard to contextualize many of the events without knowing other things in relationship to them. I know that Voat doesn't require verification or anything of that sort, but I put together a small collection of pictures that you can see here: https://slimgur.com/album/E0 -- the before-and-after photos of the surgical wound are included.

Ask me anything.
[IAMA] Person who cheated death numerous times in the past fourteen months.

That sounds crazy... how have you changed as a person from the experience? Outlook/philosophy on life etc? Your relationship with your wife?

Thanks for doing the AMA here :)

The outlook/philosophy is sort of a mixed bag. There are some pros, some cons, as it is with everything. I think one of the most significant changes is the fact that when I hear of someone's death, there's this part of me that says, "It should have been me. Why wasn't it me? Why did I survive?" One of the first things I recall from emerging out of the medically induced coma was the news of Robin Williams' suicide. I had so many people telling me how close I was to dying, and here I was hearing about someone who had. Someone who is beloved by millions of people. And even in the Intensive Care Unit (ICU), people were dying everyday. How can anyone process these questions of mortality? I could have died, and the person in the next room could have died, but it was him, not me. Why? I don't know. It could have so easily been me over him.

In response to the relationship between my wife, I am not going to lie, things were really hard for a while. Especially living with my parents. My wife and my mother are cordial with one another, but tension has always existed, and it was amplified by the fact that my wife was my legal guardian and made all of the medical decisions, and not my parents (who disagreed with a lot of choices that my wife made). I know this veers away from how it affected my marriage, but it is very much related in the sense that I was stuck in the middle a lot of the time. Not just in terms of them fighting about things related to my circumstances, but also the conflicting obligations of defending both the person who gave birth to me, and the person I plan on spending the rest of my life with. I hope this answers your question.

That was an amazing read. All I can ask is;

Are you okay now?

Well, the word "okay" is subjective. So, I suppose if you are asking whether or not I could still die from this, then the answer is "probably not." I would say, "no," but I was informed of a rare case in which someone went through it twice.

In terms of functioning as a normal human being, the answer is "not yet." My physical therapist told me that, generally, it takes one week to recover for each day you spend in the hospital. For instance, if you spend 3 days there, you will be right as rain in three weeks. I spent 174 days in the hospital. That's well over three years. I had been in a wheelchair at the beginning of the year, and then transitioned to a walker, and then to a cane, and now I can walk on my own (so long as it is not a really long distance). I have some balance issues. I can't run. I can't lift things that would be more than about ten pounds. I'm still coping with a lot of the psychological distress. But, you know how it is. It's the "one-day-at-a-time" sort of thing.

Do you remember anything while you were being mechanically ventilated? I'm a respiratory therapist and have always wondered how it feels to be sedated and ventilated.

Also, if you have any questions about my field (mechanical ventilation, tracheostomies, etc.,) I'd be happy to do my best to answer them for you!

Though I never heard the term "mechanically ventilated," I am pretty sure I know what you are referring to, and the answer is both. There was a time where I was completely unconscious and unaware of it. But I did eventually regain consciousness, and was 100% aware of the experience. Which is absolutely awful, by the way. I would have respiratory therapists coming in all of the time, performing suction on the hole in my neck. It was a very strange experience because I could not see what it looked like, and it seemed like there was a giant vacuum cleaner attached to my body.

One of my worst experiences at Hospital #2 involved a respiratory therapist. When I finally had a speaking valve, they were very much insistent about not having it on while I slept. Which was somewhat difficult to do because I was under the influence of heavy narcotics that made me drowsy, and I would drift off to sleep a lot. But one particular respiratory therapist was very upset whenever this happened. So, she actually came into my hospital room in the middle of the night and confiscated my speaking valve from me. So, when I had to notify nurses, I did not have the ability to tell them what I needed. She never brought it back, and the morning shift nurses had to actually track down that particular speaking valve, or a replacement for it. I'm not entirely certain if they gave me the same one. All I know is that they had to go find one for me because of that particular person.

But, yes, I do remember it, and I wish I could forget.

It pretty much is a vacuum cleaner. The suction has to be done like that because you aren't able to clear respiratory secretions any other way. It's uncomfortable, but helps.

As far as the valve goes, most of the manufacturers recommend against their use during sleep. It just hasn't been studied much. Also, the risk and liabilities are high because there are certain airway abnormalities that could lead to a device malfunction, potentially causing harm or death. Still no excuse to take it away and not make sure you know it's within reach.

I do understand the rationale behind it being done. It's not an objection that I have or anything. It's just that you asked about the experience, and the honest answer is, well, I hated it. The fact that it was uncomfortable was really half of the issue, with the other half being that sort of "imagination" part. I know there's a hole in my neck, and I know there's a buildup of all that junk inside, but since I am unable to really see it, my mind envisions it as a million times worse than it probably is. Does that make sense?

As far as the sleeping with the speaking valve on, I totally get it. But I had little control over when I slept. I was always drifting off with all of the IV medications. I would have rather had the nurses simply kept and eye on it, and if they saw that I had started to sleep, to just take it off for me and set it on the table next to my bed.

Yeah, that makes sense. It's really hard for me to imagine being in a situation like that with no background in the medical field. I normally talk my patients through the process and try to reassure them, but it's hard to judge coherence sometimes.

Those times when you were feeling anxious about everything going on, was there anything that a healthcare provider did for you that made you feel better emotionally?

I responded to a previous question in regards to the "emotional Hell" and the hospital psychologist who was one of the most wonderful people that I met throughout my hospitalization. So, if you just glossed over it, going back to read that would be one example

There are a few more people who were really great, too. I was actually shifted around a lot, so I got to know a lot of different staff, and my family likes to joke about how the only place they never put me was in the maternity ward. I was even on the cancer ward for a little while, just because they had run out of beds on the unit where I was supposed to be. Which, by the way, if given an option, I would say that, as a patient, it doesn't get any better than the cancer ward (provided that you don't actually have cancer). I found that many of the nurses are very accommodating and seem to be specifically trained in making one's quality of life as pleasant as it can be.

My experience in the Progressive Care Unit (PCU) was also one of the better places I stayed, and I have a really funny story about that. For a long time, I was not permitted any food or drink. Doctors' orders. For months, everything was fed into my body via tubes. But one night shift nurse working PCU asked me if I would be interested in a Popsicle, and I absolutely was. And I cannot even explain how orgasmic that was, to taste something for the first time in a very long time. This may sound strange, but it was the very first moment during my hospitalization that made me feel even remotely normal. Upon reflection, it had that sort of "home" feeling that I had not had in months. We agreed to keep "the secret Popsicle" between us. But then during crossover in the morning, we let the next nurse in on it, and she too started smuggling Popsicles for me, as well. And, again, that night during crossover, we recruited another nurse. Pretty soon, "the secret Popsicles" had spread and was a secret that was shared with half of the staff in the unit. My nurse practitioner eventually discovered what was going on, and he was somewhat bemused by the situation, and just said, "Whatever. If you can keep it down, it's fine. Just don't overdo it." So, that was definitely something that was more healing than probably anything else I had experienced.

There were also two other people worth mentioning. The first was a nurse who would come in and just have conversations with me. We would talk about our pets, and she would show me tons of pictures of her dog, and we sort of bonded over our love for animals. (Man, those service dogs that came to visit always brought my spirits up, too!) The second person was not a nurse or a doctor. Merely a med tech. But she was so kind and compassionate. One evening, I had a massive panic attack while she was nearby, and she just came over and held my hand and started talking me through everything that was going on. It meant so much to me. I would later have her as a med tech when I returned months later, and a part of me really wanted to express my gratitude. But the courage just wasn't there, and it ultimately became a missed opportunity. That might be my one regret. Since she was merely a med tech, I imagine that her job is probably a thankless one most days. And I really should have said, "thank you." That sort of gesture might have meant as much to her as her gesture meant to me. I really wish I had said something. Perhaps I can rectify this mistake in the future by ensuring that "thank yous" should be issued when an act of kindness warrants one.

You're right; I missed where you had mentioned the psychologist. Sorry about that.

I've worked with a few nurses that have worked with cancer patients and I agree, they are overall much more compassionate and in touch with the human element than some other nurses can be.

That's hilarious about the Popsicles.

As far as the med tech and the other excellent care you received, you could send a card to the hospital and mention them specifically if you know their names. That's something that always makes me feel like I'm doing the right thing and lets me know that I made a difference to someone.

No worries. It prompted me to start thinking about all of the other staff members that I appreciated. I know the first and last name of the psychologist, so she would be very easy to track down. As for the med tech, I know her first name, and the unit she works in. That might be doable. As for the nurse... uh, well... I remember the name of her dog. I might have to hire a private investigator for that one.

Another afterthought regarding someone I liked: since I had a lot of downtime, I was able to get a TV/VCR set up sent to my room because nobody wanted it (you can actually see it in the background of the "puzzle" photo in my album) and I still have like a hundred VHS tapes that my family would bring for me to watch. But there was some guy -- not even sure what his position really was -- that would come into my room occasionally to do things like make sure sheets and stuff were stocked. But every single time he came in, he'd pause for a minute and just catch a minute or two of whatever I was watching, and every time he would say, "Dude, you have the best taste in movies." I really liked that guy a lot.
